analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "E. Dugan et al. Petitioners versus Everett G. Rank. Number 51, Claude E. Rowe. That's the City of Fresno, rather. Petitioner versus California et al. And number 115, the Delano Early Mart Irrigation District et al. Petitioners versus Everett G. Rank et al. May I please the Court? This is one of three cases here on certiorari to the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, all growing out of a single action brought against the United States and officials of the Bureau of Reclamation, the central issue is whether the action, in all its aspects, is in reality a suit against the United States, barred by sovereign immunity. Our position is that it is such an action, and is so barred, and that the plaintiffs have a remedy for damages under the Tucker Act in a suit in the Court of Clans, but that they are not entitled to this action for specific relief under the doctrine of the Larson case and Malone and Bowden. The justices who were on the court at the time of the Gerlach and Ivanhoe cases will recall the complexity and grandeur of the Central Valley project. The north half of the Central Valley in California, the Sacramento Valley, has a surplus of water. The south half, the San Joaquin Valley, has a shortage of water. The purpose of the project, in essence, was to improve the use of water in both halves of the valley, but also particularly to bring the surplus down to the water-hungry regions in the San Joaquin. For present purposes, there are only two units of the project that are important to us. Both were the key units, in effect. The San Joaquin River rises in the Sierras, in the area just south of the Yosemite, and then flows southwesterly and breaks through the mountains here at Friant. Then it continues on, flowing a little bit more to the west, and then takes a sharp bend up to the northwest, and in the delta area, it joins the Sacramento, and the two flow out through the Golden Gate you see. The first unit that we're concerned with is the Friant Dam, which was built right here where the river breaks through the mountains, and behind which is Millerton Lake, a storage reservoir. Extending from that dam, north is the Madeira Canal, and south the Friant Turn Canal, which transport water to regions that otherwise would be shortage areas. And they take, when the dam is closed, all, or virtually all, the water of the San Joaquin. The irrigation districts, which are the petitioners in the third case to be heard today, are the districts that are furnished by these two canals. One runs about 50 miles, and the other about 150. Closing the Friant Dam and diverting the water via the canal would, of course, unless something else were done, cut off the irrigation water available to the lower San Joaquin belt. To take care of that, we have the second significant unit of the project here, the Delta Mendota Canal, which runs from the Delta, where it hooks on to the Sacramento River, comes to the pumping plant of Tracy, is then raised and flows by gravity down here to a place called Mendota Pool. There it is released and flows back up north again and waters these lands which previously received water of the San Joaquin River. No, there are maps in the briefs. See, I should think we could as quickly as we can, as we can, certainly, as quickly as we can, yes. And I think there's another that I'm sure I can obtain copies of that are somewhat easier than the briefs. You will? Certainly will, yes. Except for getting it reproduced, if we have to. We'll have to make up our minds which way to do it. We'll try to get it reproduced and then we're carrying this along with the reproduction. You'll have noticed, of course, that since the Delta Mendota Canal comes only to Delta Pool, this would mean that if Friant Dam were closed to Flicka, this area on which I've marked the grid of running from Friant Dam down to Mendota Pool would be without water. And that is the area that we're concerned with in this case. the diversion of the natural flow at the San Joaquin, having made no provision for those lands in the red area, gave rise to a problem that the Reclamation Bureau and the United States, of course, had faced. Some of the water rights in that area, indeed most of the water rights in that area, were acquired under state law. We entered into contracts either buying the rights or contracts to supply them with water or agreed a partial arrangement to supply some water and to make some payment. A minority of the landowners and the United States were unable to agree and this suit resulted. The water rights asserted by the plaintiffs were of three kinds. Some of the plaintiffs, whose land is actually along the river, claimed riparian rights, which California still recognizes to a degree. The United States has always acknowledged some interference with those riparian rights. It claims to have taken them to the extent that there is interference and it denies the full amount of the interference that the plaintiffs claim. Some of the plaintiffs claim what are known as overlying rights to the underground waters, which they claim were fed by the San Joaquin River. They were mostly in this area, south of the river, barely reaching to the city of Fresno. The United States, for the most part, denies that it has interfered with the overlying rights to the extent that they have been impaired. Again, we claim to have taken them. Some of the plaintiffs, I should say, too, that the city of Fresno has been spoken of for the most part as being in the category of the owner of overlying rights. Finally, some of the plaintiffs claim appropriative rights. That is to say, they are not, neither overlying landowners nor riparian, but they claim to have taken water and put it to beneficial use in time to have acquired rights under California water law. The action was brought by the plaintiffs against the... Oh, yes. Subject to only one... Subject to one possible qualification, and I don't... We don't have enough facts to say how much of a qualification it is. Some of them may now be barred by the statute of limitations. Although most of them have already brought their suits and were not barred by the statute. But I wouldn't want to say that there was nobody who might be barred by the statute. But we acknowledged to the extent we'd interfered that we were clearly bound to recognize the rights under state law to that extent that we had to take them. We couldn't just wipe them out. And that that gave rise to an obligation to take. So the real issue here isn't one of the obligation to pay. It's of whether they can tie up the project as a way of asserting their rights. The action was brought against officials of the Reclamation Bureau to seek what is called a physical solution of the plaintiffs' originally riparian rights. Under California law, a riparian or overlying owner who can show that other people on the stream are interfering with the natural flow of the water may obtain a decree restraining interference with the flow of the stream unless the junior appropriator at his own expense makes some physical arrangements which will protect the superior right of the riparian owner to water to a reasonable extent. For example, in the present case, which is as good an example of a physical solution as any, the district court enjoined the operation of Friant Dam, said you can't use Friant Dam, and required the Reclamation Bureau to release all the waters of the San Joaquin River unless the United States built a series of ten more dams and operated them in the manner that the district court required, describing the dams in great detail, even down to gantry cranes and the size rails that the cranes should run on and so forth, and it provided that there should be a specified flow of water over the last dam. The individual defendants, when the suit was started, moved to dismiss upon various grounds, but especially on the ground that the action was in reality one against the United States barred under the doctrine of the Larson case. When that motion was denied, the officials made a number of answers, including answers on the merits, but they preserved the position, which we insist upon here at all times, that this was an unconsented-to suit against the United States. The district court found against the reclamation officials, both on the question of jurisdiction and on the merits. It entered a decree, which, as I have said, enjoined the operation of Friant Dam, enjoined the transfer of water through the Madeira and Friant-Pern canals, unless the United States, which it recognized would have to go in, chose to build ten additional dams on this stretch of the river down to Gravely Ford at an expense of somewhere around the million dollars. I must now, I think, for the purposes of clarification, turn to a second aspect of the case in the district court. The city of Fresno was one of the plaintiffs in the original action, seeking protection of what Fresno said were her overlying rights to the underground waters, alleged by her but denied by us as coming from the San Joaquin. At this stage, when Fresno came in, the United States was joined as a defendant, or at least attempted to be joined, because the United States never appeared. In addition, Fresno filed a separate complaint and intervention against both the Reclamation Bureau officials and the United States, seeking a declaratory judgment that her right to take additional water from the San Joaquin River, from the natural flow, was superior to any rights of the United States to the waters of the San Joaquin, because we had acquired assignments of rights to the waters of the San Joaquin from the state of California. Third, Fresno sought a declaratory judgment that the United States was obliged to furnish Fresno with water from Millerton Lake behind Friant Dam at the price of $3.50 an acre foot, although the price charged all other municipalities for water under the Central Valley project is higher and ranges up, but not above, $10 an acre foot. The District Court gave judgment against the United States on both these claims for a declaratory judgment. The Court of Appeals reversed as to the United States, holding that there was an unconsented to suit against the United States, and the City of Fresno, by the petition in No. 51, the second case to be argued today, brought that ruling here. with respect to the original suit, the Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment in favor of the riparian overlying owners so far as the individual defendants were concerned. It held it was not an action, really an action against the United States, because it fell within the exception which permits, it said, suits against officers of the United States, where they are acting outside of the scope of their authority and committing a tort against the plaintiffs. Was Fresno a plaintiff in that suit? Fresno was a plaintiff in that suit. So the Fresno really has three claims. It's in common with all the overlying owners and riparian owners. It has its claim that it's entitled to a declaration that it has a right to appropriate water out of the natural flow ahead of any rights of the United States. And that's No. 51 here. That's No. 51 here. And it has a declaration which is also in No. 51 that it's entitled to water at 350 an acre foot. On the Reclamation Bureau's petition, which I'm going to address myself now, we submit that the courts below both erred in failing to dismiss the action as an unconsented to suit against the United States. Certainly it is such a suit in every substantial respect. The Bureau officials were sued only to control their action as officers of the United States. The complaint sought not damages but an injunctive decree granting specific relief. Under the decree, either Friant Dam must stand idle, the great works unused, no water flowing either north or south through the Madeira Canal or the Friant-Pern Canal, and no water supplied to the irrigation district. Or else, excuse me, if you agree with us in this position, there is nothing left to decide. Oh, well, we would have a, we have essentially the same position but the reasoning is a little different. In 51, we claim it's a suit against the United States and indeed we think it obviously is. and the question there is whether, the only question so far as I can see, is whether the United States has given its consent. There is an argument that the United States has consented to be sued. And I suppose that if that argument is good, it really takes care of 31-2. So I guess that the court has to decide a minimum of two points. one, whether Larson and Malone and Bowdoin are decisive in that general principle. And second, whether Section 206A of an act of 1950 known as the McCarran Amendment gives consent to suits against the United States. I was saying that the decree that this suit was in substance against the United States, either it expends itself on these key units of the Central Valley Project and prevents its operation, or in the alternative, it compels the United States, and this is admitted, to build ten more dams on the river which have not been approved by the Reclamation Bureau and which have not been authorized and for which no money has been appropriated by Congress. The order, in a suit against the United States, there's no such case. No such case. As among private parties in California law there is pressed. But I know of no case anywhere near this. You mean to say that if the government is putting up a dam that will flood my house that I'm without any remedy to stop them from doing it unless they condemn it? Well, I think that when they put up the dam and flood the house they have condemned it. But, I mean, if they take no measures to acquire the land within the project... The very fact of putting up... Well, if the project is unauthorized, if the Reclamation Bureau... Oh, it's authorized. Well, if it's authorized, then as in the Gerlach case... A government official never can be a trespasser? Well, if he's authorized he can't be a trespasser, no. So there's no such thing as a suit against an official than the government? There's no such... There's no permitted suit against an official of the government acting within his authority. That seems to me to be the lesson... Why doesn't the government... The government has... The government is much more powerful than the individual. Well, they can condemn, can't they? Why don't they condemn? Well, the government... The government, when it builds the dam and cuts off the rights, does condemn, as it did in Gerlach. That was the holding of the court in Gerlach. Similarly, in many flowage cases, the government, when it erects a dam or a lock and it flows the land behind, that flowing constitutes a taking then and there and an action will lie for it. Under the tuck right. Under the tuck right, yes. This affords a remedy, but at the same time, it permits the government to go forward with the work. Yes, if a person is timely in his suit and so on. Well, true, but the Dickinson case, I think, indicates that there is no barring of his cause of action if there is genuine uncertainty or lack of knowledge as to whether there really has been any taking. And it would seem to me that the same was true here. That if a man could show that there was a taking here. What? You think it is doubtful that there was a taking? Well, you see, the essence, I think there was clearly some taking. And the, I, there was no taking by judicial proceedings. It was the kind of taking that there was in the girl out there. And there was clearly some taking. Now, there's some dispute has been from the beginning as to just how much of this underground water was affected by the closing of Fry and Dan. We don't say there was a taking to the, as to those parts which we claim were not affected. On the other hand, we say anything that was affected was clearly taken just as it was in the Gerlach case. And that the issue as to where that line is cannot be tried out in a suit to interfere with the operation of the project. Because we think these officials clearly acted within their authority as between principal and agent when they constructed the dam. the trial court held that there was no taking. The court of appeals held we had authority to take but that there was no taking. The court of appeals said that there could be no taking unless one were more precise in telling the plaintiffs exactly what had been taken. Now, we say as to that that it doesn't matter whether there was a taking or not. Well, we really say three things, Mr. Justice Clark. We say first that there was a taking. We think that if you look at the case in terms of could anyone in this area sue the United States for a taking under the Gerlach case, the answer would unquestionably be yes. And that if there was a taking to that purpose, there was a taking to the purposes of our case. Second, we say that it doesn't matter whether there was a taking or not, or exactly how much was taken at this stage because of the doctrine of the Larson case and Malone and Boone. Because here certainly these defendants were acting within the scope of their authority. They were, I think the confusion arises from the term acting within the scope of their authority. It's possible for example to say that, well, the officer in the forest service, that no officer in the forest service is authorized to take somebody else's land and to oust them from possession and to claim under a void deed. If one posits it as a known and indisputable truth that he is taking land that belongs to someone else and that he knows that and knows the deed to be void, then I suppose he is acting outside the scope of his authority. But of course, that's right. I was simply using this for illustrative purposes. But he is authorized to determine what land he thinks belongs to the United States in his best judgment. That's what the United States sets him up to do. And when he makes that decision, whether he is right or wrong does not destroy his authority. And that's the reason that the action for ejectment wouldn't lie in Malone and Bowdoin. Similarly, in the Larson case, I take it that everyone would agree that Larson, the war assets administrator, wasn't authorized to sell coal to A, then knowing he'd sold it to A and the title had passed, he was obligated to make delivery to sell it to B. But on the other hand, he was authorized to superintend the administration of contracts and to interpret them. And provided he acts in his good judgment, and perhaps not capriciously, his decision is not placed outside his authority. I'd always suppose that the land cases had a special place in this court's decision for protection of the Lee, according to the Lee case. Well, it would seem to me that I'm not, I think it's very, it's gone very largely in a case where an action will lie under the tuckerer, and that Malone and Bowdoin shows there is no special protection for land cases in the Larson case dealt with channels. Now here, in this situation, the officers the court below held were authorized to take this, any water rights necessary, or to take any land necessary for this project. They were also certainly authorized to operate the dam and to interfere with the natural flow, where it didn't interfere with anyone's rights. Those were judgments that they were empowered to make. Whether they made some mistake in them may have resulted in their committing a tort, but it did not deprive them of the authority to act. And really, the holding of the court below and the plaintiff's argument, it seems to me, comes down to a contention that this special category of cases still exists, that an officer of the United States may be enjoined when he has been committing a common law of tort. I was just going to say that that category of case was held non-existent in Larson, that that is not ground pursuing an officer of the United States, and that if there could be any doubt after Larson, as apparently there was, because the Fifth Circuit in the case, and the Ninth Circuit in this case, rendered inconsistent decisions, they were set straight in Bowdoin so far as the Fifth Circuit was concerned. Frankly, I can't believe the Ninth Circuit would have decided this case did, had Malone and Bowdoin been available to it at that time. Yes? My question is going to be, what has happened in the physical construction of this project during the pendency of this suit? Has it all been stopped? No, no. There was a period when it was operated under consent decrees. The Friant Dam was built, the water districts are being searched. In point of fact, the government's arrangement with some of the owners between Friant Dam and Gravely Four, the area we're preserving, because we acquired all these rights below Gravely Four. the government entered into an arrangement with a number of owners saying that it would let down specified quantities of water up to five cubic feet a second regularly. And it entered into arrangements with them to build channels, putting pumps to make other things. So as a result of the settlement with the people who aren't here, a certain amount of water has been going down. We think indeed, but this is hotly disputed and the court found against us, we think indeed that's enough to take care of all the riparian rights. The owners of overlying rights are still pumping water. The water table is going down. In their view and in the district court's view, this is a result of what we've done with Friant Dam. In our view, it isn't a result of that at all. Of course, we can't argue that issue here, and I mention it only to find out that what we're objecting to is trying that issue not in a Tucker Act suit where it belonged, but in an action that plainly expends itself on the property and treasury of the United States. I would like to... included within the project and the proof of the Congress, wasn't it? This is within the project as approved by the Congress. These specific incidents were described during the 50s, the exact references are in my brief, to the Congress and the Congress voted appropriation to make settlements with those fellows that we've settled with downstream. They knew exactly what we were doing. I remember it. It was in Ivanhoe, wasn't it? I wrote Ivanhoe. Yes. Didn't we discuss the front dam and the cementer in which it... You had to mention it both in Ivanhoe and particularly in Gerlach, because you'll remember in Gerlach the word writes down here on the San Joaquin. Just a Jackson, will it? Yes. Just a Jackson. In summary, because I'm afraid I've jumped around a bit, let me simply state the three objections to the decree of the judgment of the Ninth Circuit that I've tried to refer to. First, we think there was a taking, and that issue will be argued by the Irrigation District, and it may be that in the Fresno case, I'll have some time to refer to it. Second, we say even if there wasn't a taking, even if there's uncertainty as to what was taken and what was interfered with and what wasn't interfered with at all, that the action is in reality won against the United States, because the gist of the claim is that this was a tort. And we deny the tort, but that's an issue that can't be tried out, we say, in this kind of action. If it was a tort, would the Court of Claims have jurisdiction? Not if it was simply a tort. Because it's clearly not within the Federal Tort Claims Act. Clearly not within the Federal Tort Claims Act. It's not within the Tucker Act. If it's so little of a tort as not to amount to a taking, yes. I find it very difficult to think there was such a thing, to tell you the truth, Mr. Justice Stewart. I think either we did one, either we took, or we didn't affect it at all. But I think in theory, if there is a zone in between, which the government has never been very successful in Tucker Act cases in arguing that there was, and quite rightly in my judgment, if there is a zone in between, there would be no remedy. That would be the right of it. But we're not arguing that the Tucker Act should be so narrowly construed here. We're objecting to the specific relief. The third point, if I might take 30 seconds, the third point that we say is that both the majority and dissenting opinions in Larson say that even where an officer has been acting outside his authority, that if the decree would compel affirmative action by the United States, or expend itself upon the property of the United States, then the action for the injunction will not lie. And we think this case falls for reasons stated in our brief in that category. That's right. That's right. You took some water or no water? We interfered with some flow of water or we didn't interfere with it, one or the other. And if there was no taking, there was no grounds for the injunction? There was no grounds for an injunction. Of course, that just... Right. And that that's the proper place without interfering with the... Not in this lawsuit. Right. Right. Right. Right. This honorable court, you have, I believe, presented to you a large green brief by the city of Fresno in which most of the acts of Congress involving the Central Valley Project are listed. At the start, I would like to make a correction and state that we do not agree with the map before this court. this so-called river from that point down here does not exist. And... But I missed that. I'm sorry. What did you say? I missed what you just said. Could you repeat? I said, uh, the San Joaquin River according to the... Well, what I just said, this river from there to here does not exist. And, uh, that will come up in the state's argument. It's the city's position. The map is incorrect. Now, I don't... I don't... Well, I will show you. There is no such stream from here to this square nor from the square to this other so-called lake. And if it is not, uh, out of line to, uh, it just does not exist. It never existed as a natural channel. Now, that is shown by Exhibit 6, uh, opposite page 86 of the Green Brief. I don't know whether it's proper to mention the Chief Justice's name, but his name appears on the cover of that bulletin that that map was printed on. So I think that's, if it's proper to mention his name, I think that's pretty good, uh, evidence that the stream does not exist as a natural stream. What brief is that in? That is in the Green Brief, the large green brief. Which number case? Uh, 51. 51. Yes. I don't know what you mean as a natural stream. Is there a bed of a river there? No. In other words, uh, this was put in, I think, in an effort to avoid the, and a sincere effort, I'm not, uh, it is our position. This is the Kern River. The Kern River terminates in Buena Vista Lake. There's no natural waterway from there to Tulare Lake. There is an artificial waterway, but this indicates it's a natural stream, and that therefore possibly the Kern River is in the watershed of the San Joaquin. They also attempt to connect that to the San Joaquin. I would like to point out a map as Exhibit 2, opposite page, uh, 16 of the Green Brief, which is prepared for the District Court, uh, in the decision below, and that map prepared by the United States Bureau of Reclamation does not show any stream from Buena Vista Lake to Tulare Lake. Now, that, uh, will, I think that point may become important later in the argument. Why? Can you tell us in the words? Yes. In California, according to the fundamental law, the county of origin and watersheds of origin are to receive all necessary water before any water is exported out of the watershed or the county of origin. Now, Fresno lies in Fresno County, which is founded by this stream on the south and by the San Joaquin on the north. The Act of Congress of October 14, 1949, specifically requires the Bureau of Reclamation and the Secretary of the Interior to recognize the county and watershed of origin acts in the operation of the central valley project. Part of the city of Fresno's, uh, complaint is based upon, it is in the county of origin of the San Joaquin River and in the watershed of the San Joaquin River where this water originates. So that under state law and under the Act of October 14, 1949, Fresno and these landowners in the watershed of the San Joaquin have specifically been given water to the extent of their needs before the Secretary can attempt to import that water out of the county and watershed of origin. Now, the district court found that Larry County, which lies south of Fresno County and Kern County down here, were not in the watershed of the San Joaquin River. I do not believe that was distinctly appealed. It may have been, but the district court so found that the Kings River here, they were at one time two inland seas, one here and one here, that the Kern River drains into Buena Vista Lake and stops, that these other rivers in Tulare and Kern County drain into Tulare Lake. Due to levees of Buena Vista Lake and an artificial channel, waters have been forced to run into Tulare Lake and by levees here have been forced maybe twice in 100 years to run into the San Joaquin River. There is a bed there then. What did you say? There is a riverbed there. The riverbed, there is no riverbed. There is an artificial channel. There are some sloughs and an artificial channel, but in determining a watershed, I believe under the law, a watershed is determined by natural channels, that you cannot put yourself in the watershed by digging a ditch over into another watershed. It comes in below gravity, it's fuller, doesn't it? What did you say? I'm not sure I can see it too well. Does the Kern River come into San Joaquin according to the map? This is the Kern River, Your Honor. Now on up north. That is Buena Vista Lake. On up north now. Trace it on up north. That little line. Then it goes right on into San Joaquin below the Grand La Forge, doesn't it? Grand La Forge. Yes. The law is also clear. I think that a watershed in this area is not assuming that is true. A watershed down here is not in the watershed at the area above the junction. I didn't understand the government claimed that, but perhaps I'm wrong. Well, I don't know whether the government does or not. I think the district did. I get your point, though. In other words, they first come out and said that they were empowered to take the water from the city of Fresno and county of Fresno's watershed. And even though they needed it and were entitled to it, both under state law and the acts of Congress, they could take it out here. I think they've abandoned that position. Maybe not. They now, under the authorities, they're attempting to come in, you might say, the back door and claim they're in the watershed. They have relied on state bulletin 29, which is one of the bases of the Central Valley Projects when the state of California took it over. And that bulletin, as quoted in my recovery to the government and to the districts, that the districts have raised that point, the government didn't raise it in their brief, states that the Kern River watershed is in Tulare and Kern County. At the watershed, the San Joaquin is in Fresno County. But I point that out. Now, the government did not raise that point. I had one question. Yes. I was not clear in your brief. I didn't, it wasn't clear to me on this point. Do you admit that the federal government can take this water from Fresno? No. I didn't take you there. My, or our position is this, that the state of California, by decisions of the Supreme Court of the state of California, and by two statutes, give protection to the county and watershed of origin, that by the Reclamation Act of 1902, the government must proceed in accord with state laws in their operation of the reclamation project. But to clear that up, beyond all doubt, Congress, on October 14, 1949, the act is quoted in my brief, specifically enjoined the Secretary of the Interior to proceed and conform to all California county of origin and watershed protected matters. So, therefore, our position, they cannot take it.
